articles.title: After war took her leg, this Ukrainian gymnast refused to give up
articles.summary: When 10-year-old Ukrainian gymnast Sasha Paskal stepped onto the stage in New York's Times Square this week, she carried a message far bigger than her performance.
articles.content:
After surviving a Russian attack that claimed her leg, Sasha now hopes her story will remind the world that Ukraine's children are still living through war.

Ahead of her performance – she’s a rhythmic gymnast specializing in choreographed routines – Sasha and her mother, Maria, visited UN Headquarters, where they spoke to UN News about resilience, recovery and why, above all, children need peace.

Photo courtesy of the Pascal family

Bouncing back

Sasha had been training in rhythmic gymnastics since early childhood when her life changed dramatically in 2022.

During the early months of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, she was seriously injured in an attack in the Odesa region.

A collapsing concrete slab crushed the bones in her leg, leaving doctors with no choice but to amputate the limb after she spent 15 days in a medically induced coma.

Following months of rehabilitation, Sasha returned to the sport she loves, performing dance and acrobatic routines with a modern prosthetic leg.

Over the past four years, she has competed alongside children without disabilities, winning medals at several competitions, including most recently an international tournament in Romania.

Children need peace

For Maria, every performance is an opportunity to keep international attention focused on Ukraine's children.

“The main message is that people should not forget that the war is still going on in our country,” she said.

What Ukrainian children need most, she added, is peace.

Sasha's story has also inspired The Heart Sees More Than the Eyes, an inclusive comic book created by young people with support from UNICEF, the UN’s children agency, through the UPSHIFT programme.

The comic follows a young gymnast who continues training after losing a leg and is used in classroom activities that encourage children to better understand disability and inclusion.

Toll on children

Sasha's experience reflects the wider toll the war continues to take on Ukraine's children.

According to UNICEF, nearly 2.6 million children – more than one-third of all children in Ukraine – remain displaced from their homes. Around 791,000 are internally displaced within the country, while another 1.8 million are living as refugees abroad.

Since February 2022, more than 3,400 children have been killed or injured in attacks, although the true number is believed to be significantly higher because many cases cannot be independently verified.

The war has also disrupted education, with more than 1,700 schools and educational facilities damaged or destroyed.

One in three are still unable to attend school in person full time, while children living near the frontlines face particularly severe psychological impacts.

UNICEF and its partners continue to provide humanitarian assistance, psychosocial support, education services and programmes that help children recover from the effects of war.

Strength through sport

Today, Sasha trains for three to four hours a day, five days a week. Her mother believes gymnastics has been essential to her recovery.

“I think that without sport, everything would have been much worse,” Maria said. “She would have withdrawn into herself and been ashamed of her prosthetic leg. But when she competes, she isn't embarrassed. She becomes much more confident.”

Photo courtesy of the Pascal family

Looking ahead, Sasha dreams of one day representing Ukraine at the Paralympic Games if rhythmic gymnastics is included in the programme.

Although she admits she still gets nervous before competitions, she has simple advice for other children facing challenges.

“Don't give up and keep moving forward,” she said. “And don't be afraid of anything.”

articles.title: Losing my leg has elevated my life, says world champion surfer
articles.summary: Llywelyn Williams says anything is possible with any kind of disability.
articles.content:
Four-time world champion adaptive surfer Llywelyn Williams says losing his leg as a teenager elevated his life.

Surfing played a pivotal role in his recovery and in the years since losing a leg after being hit by a car in 2011.

It had been a passion of the then 16-year-old prior to the accident - and it was not going to stop him despite being severely injured while out skateboarding.

In fact, he recalled coming around from a coma in hospital amid a dream that a surfboard came between him and a bright light "like you see in the movies".

"It wasn't my time," said Williams, from Abersoch, Gwynedd.

A friend asked him what he wanted to do while he lay in his hospital bed; he wanted to get back in the water - and go surfing in Australia.

"The rehab was to drive myself to get back into the ocean," said Williams, known as Sponge by friends.

"As soon as I got back in the ocean, I felt like I was born again.

"When the board and you connect perfect on the wave, it just feels like you're flying."
articles.reasoning: The article highlights an inspiring story of overcoming disability and finding empowerment through adaptive sports, promoting hope and resilience for people with disabilities. It has broad societal significance by challenging perceptions and encouraging inclusion.

**What happened** – At 16, Llywelyn was severely injured in a skateboarding accident. While in a coma, he dreamed of a surfboard shielding him from a bright light, which gave him hope. After waking, he focused on one goal: to return to surfing. With determination, he worked through rehabilitation, driving himself to get back into the ocean and eventually surfed again.

**Impact** – Llywelyn’s story shows how losing a leg did not stop him from achieving greatness in surfing. His return to the sport helped him heal and gave him a new sense of freedom and joy. It also challenges common ideas about disabilities, showing that people can still follow their dreams and succeed.

**What's next step** – Llywelyn plans to keep surfing and inspiring others with disabilities to try adaptive sports. His example encourages more people to believe in their abilities and push past challenges.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After losing his leg, Llywelyn Williams used surfing to transform his life and become a world champion in adaptive sports.

articles.title: 'This is just the start': India's Gen Z protesters force out a minister, but what next?
articles.summary: The education minister's resignation, a rare setback for the Modi government, brings hope to many young protesters that their voices will be heard.
articles.content:
In 12 years of Narendra Modi's rule in India , only one cabinet minister had previously resigned - over allegations of sexual misconduct.

So education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation on Saturday, after more than a week of intense street protests, became a defining moment - one many young people celebrated as a rare victory.

In the words of 22-year-old Sakhi, a student activist in Delhi, "for the first time, it felt like we can make things happen through protests".

Soon after Pradhan quit, social media seized on an old video of a senior Modi minister boasting that "resignations do not happen in our government", reflecting the confidence of the nationwide youth movement that had demanded his exit.

Sakhi says they grew up reading textbooks that spoke about the importance of dissent in a democracy, "but I did not see that around me in the Modi years".

On Instagram, Sakhi posted photos and videos of police assaults and detentions alongside reels mocking officers standing beside them. Many have been viewed millions of times.

Sakhi says the government failed to grasp the movement's momentum because it was out of touch with the language and platforms of the protests. "The government has a hold on mainstream media, Facebook and WhatsApp. But it missed Instagram."
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant political event where youth-led protests in India led to the resignation of a cabinet minister, marking a rare government accountability moment. This represents a meaningful victory for democratic expression and youth empowerment, with broad societal implications for political engagement and human rights.
articles.personality_title: India's young protesters win a rare government resignation
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi has been in power for 12 years, and during this time, only one cabinet minister had ever resigned before, and that was over serious misconduct allegations. This shows how rare it is for ministers to step down.

**What happened** – Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned after more than a week of strong protests led mostly by young people. These protests took place on the streets and gained a lot of attention on social media, especially Instagram. A 22-year-old student activist named Sakhi said this was the first time she felt protests could really make a difference.

**Impact** – This resignation is important because it shows that young people’s voices can lead to real change in India’s government. It challenges the idea that ministers never resign and encourages more political involvement from youth. The protests also highlighted how the government was not prepared for new forms of social media activism.

**What's next step** – The youth movement is likely to keep pushing for more changes and holding leaders accountable. The government might also need to pay more attention to social media platforms like Instagram to understand public opinion better.

**One-sentence takeaway** – For the first time in years, young protesters in India helped force a government minister to resign, showing the power of youth voices and social media activism.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le ministre de l’Éducation, Dharmendra Pradhan, a démissionné après plus d’une semaine de manifestations fortes menées surtout par des jeunes. Sakhi, une étudiante de 22 ans, a dit que c’était la première fois qu’elle sentait que les manifestations pouvaient vraiment changer les choses.

**Impact** – Cette démission est importante car elle montre que les jeunes peuvent influencer le gouvernement en Inde. Cela remet en question l’idée que les ministres ne démissionnent jamais et encourage plus d’engagement politique chez les jeunes. Les manifestations ont aussi montré que le gouvernement n’était pas préparé aux nouvelles formes d’activisme sur les réseaux sociaux.

**Prochaine étape** – Le mouvement des jeunes va probablement continuer à demander des changements et à surveiller les dirigeants. Le gouvernement devra aussi peut-être mieux comprendre les réseaux sociaux comme Instagram pour suivre l’opinion publique.

**Phrase clé** – Pour la première fois depuis des années, des jeunes manifestants en Inde ont fait démissionner un ministre, montrant la force des voix jeunes et de l’activisme sur les réseaux sociaux.

articles.title: Syria’s hopes for renewal hinge on rebuilding trust, lives and livelihoods
articles.summary: A country long known as a meeting point of civilizations, Syria stands once again at a crossroads.
articles.content:
Across Syria, the scars of war remain etched into communities that have endured years of violence, displacement and loss.

Yet amid the devastation, hopes are also taking root, hopes for security, decent jobs, functioning schools and hospitals, and a future in which people from every background feel they belong.

During a landmark visit to Damascus, UN Secretary-General António Guterres encountered both realities.

Tweet URL

He visited the notorious Sednaya prison, where thousands were tortured and killed during the conflict, listened to accounts of fear and suffering, and met representatives of Syria's diverse communities, civil society groups, women and young people seeking a stake in their country's future.

As he wrapped up his visit, the UN chief said political change must now deliver tangible improvements for all Syrians, backed by sustained international support.

This comes a day after the Secretary-General met President Ahmad Al-Sharaa and reaffirmed the United Nations’ commitment to supporting the Syrian people and working closely with the country’s authorities during a critical period of transition.

A pivotal moment

“After so much suffering, this period of transition is a rare moment in the life of a nation,” Mr. Guterres told journalists on Sunday as he concluded the second day of his visit.

“A moment of responsibility, possibility and choice.”

Describing Syria as a country at a historic turning point, the Secretary-General said people across the nation were drawing on their own experiences and aspirations to shape a new future after years of conflict.

Over the course of his visit, he said he witnessed both the deep wounds left by war and the determination of Syrians to move forward.

“During these past days, I have seen the scars left by years of conflict. I have heard about pain, loss, displacement and fear.”

But alongside those experiences, he said, he had also encountered resilience and optimism.

“I have felt a profound sense of hope.”

UN/ Ali Haj Sulieman

Diversity a source of strength

Throughout his remarks, the Secretary-General repeatedly emphasized Syria's rich diversity, describing it as one of the country's defining characteristics and a foundation for lasting peace.

“This country has long known what it means to be a crossroads – of civilizations, cultures, faiths and ideas,” he said.

“That diversity is not incidental to Syria. It is one of this country's greatest strengths.”

Mr. Guterres stressed that the success of the transition would depend on ensuring all Syrians feel represented in the country's future and can participate meaningfully in shaping it.

He said the aspirations he heard during the visit were universal: security and stability, economic opportunity, accountable institutions and respect for rights.

The United Nations, he added, stands ready to support efforts to promote accountability, reconciliation, human rights and confidence-building among communities while ensuring the participation of women, young people and all components of Syrian society.

UN/ Ali Haj Sulieman

Recovery cannot be Syria’s burden alone

The Secretary-General also used the visit to deliver a strong appeal to international partners, arguing that political change would need to be matched by significant economic support if Syrians are to see tangible improvements in their daily lives.

“The task now is to translate political change into tangible improvements in people's daily lives,” he said and added: “Every Syrian must feel equally invested in the future of the country.”

While welcoming recent steps that have eased sanctions and opened new possibilities for economic recovery, Mr. Guterres called for all remaining sanctions to be lifted immediately.

He argued that rebuilding Syria would require sustained international engagement, investment and practical assistance.

“The Syrian people have shown extraordinary resilience through years of hardship,” he said.

“They should not have to carry the burden of recovery alone.”

The Secretary-General said support was needed to restore services, rebuild infrastructure, revive livelihoods and strengthen education and healthcare systems.

International assistance would also be essential to help refugees and displaced people return home safely, voluntarily and with dignity, he added.

A steadfast partner

Looking ahead, Mr. Guterres said the road forward would not be easy and warned that setbacks were inevitable.

Yet he insisted that a rare opportunity exists to build a more inclusive and peaceful future.

“There is also a real and extraordinary opportunity,” he said, “to help build a Syria where women and men participate fully in shaping their country's future ... where young people can fulfil their aspirations ... and where every person can live in dignity, equality, security, and peace.”

“The United Nations will be a steadfast partner of the Syrian people in that journey.”

articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Siria ha enfrentado muchos años de guerra, causando daños a comunidades, hogares y vidas. A pesar de esto, la gente espera paz, empleos y la reapertura de escuelas.

**Qué pasó** – En una reciente visita a Damasco, el Secretario General de la ONU, António Guterres, se reunió con sirios de diferentes orígenes y visitó lugares afectados por el conflicto, como la prisión de Sednaya. Conversó con líderes y ciudadanos sobre sus esperanzas y desafíos.

**Impacto** – Guterres destacó la diversidad de Siria como una fortaleza para construir la paz. Subrayó que el cambio político debe traer mejoras reales, como mejor seguridad y empleos, y que todos los sirios deben participar en el futuro. También pidió a la comunidad internacional que apoye a Siria con fondos y ayuda.

**Próximo paso** – La ONU planea ayudar a Siria a reconstruir escuelas, hospitales y viviendas, y apoyar el regreso seguro de los refugiados. Se insta a la comunidad internacional a levantar las sanciones restantes y proporcionar ayuda continua para la recuperación.

**Conclusión en una frase** – La ONU trabaja con los sirios y el mundo para convertir la esperanza en progreso real, reconstruyendo confianza, servicios y oportunidades tras años de conflicto.
